snip.t: SIRS (Systemic inflammatory response syndrome): The clinical syndrome that results from a deregulated inflammatory response or to a noninfectious insult.
If unchecked: Septic cascade → Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) → Hypotension, organ dysfunction → Septic shock.
The older teaching model defined sepsis as infection plus systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS); “severe sepsis” meant sepsis with organ dysfunction.

qs.q: A 60-year-old male alcoholic presents with severe epigastric pain and signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). He is found to have necrotising pancreatitis complicated by infection and organ failure. What is the approximate expected mortality for this specific complication?
o: Low mortality rate ranging between one and five percent
High mortality rate ranging between thirty and forty percent
Moderate mortality rate ranging between ten and fifteen percent
Critical mortality rate ranging between sixty and seventy-five percent
qs.e: Infected necrosis accompanied by organ failure carries a high mortality rate of 30 to 40%. Overall severe pancreatitis has a lower baseline mortality of about 15%.

qs.q: Which of the following findings is a component of the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria?
o: Serum lactate greater than 2 mmol per liter
Platelet count less than 100,000 per microliter
Heart rate higher than 90 beats per minute
qs.e: SIRS criteria include a heart rate higher than 90/min, alongside temperature extremes, abnormal hyperventilation, and abnormal white blood cell counts. Hypotension and lactate are part of shock or organ dysfunction definitions.

qs.q: Which clinical finding is part of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria?
o: Platelet count lower than 100,000 cells per microliter
Respiratory rate greater than 25 breaths per minute
Body temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C
Systolic blood pressure less than 100 mm Hg
qs.e: SIRS criteria include body temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C, along with heart rate, respiration, and WBC abnormalities. Blood pressure thresholds are not part of the standard SIRS definition.

es.q: Define Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) and list its clinical criteria according to the provided study notes.
es.m:
- **Definition**: SIRS is an exaggerated defense response of the body to a noxious stressor such as infection, trauma, surgery, acute inflammation, ischemia, reperfusion, or malignancy.
- **Body Temperature**: Temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C.
- **Heart Rate**: Heart rate higher than 90 beats per minute.
- **Hyperventilation**: Respiratory rate higher than 20 breaths per minute or PaCO2 lower than 32 mmHg.
- **White Blood Cell Count**: WBC count greater than 12,000 cells/μl or lower than 4,000 cells/μl.
- **Clinical Threshold**: SIRS is considered present when patients have more than one of these clinical findings.

faq.a: Yes; trauma, burns, pancreatitis, severe malaria and other non‑infectious insults can meet the criteria.
Adequate perfusion improves antibiotic delivery to tissues and reduces progression to shock.
Start empiric antibiotics based on the most likely local pathogens and adjust when a specific cause is identified.

exam: What are the four clinical criteria for SIRS and why must at least two be present? — Shows understanding of diagnostic thresholds and avoids over‑diagnosis.

A 28‑year‑old with HIV presents with fever, tachycardia, and a respiratory rate of 24; no obvious infection. What is your next step? — Emphasises early broad assessment and source‑search before labeling sepsis.
How does severe malaria mimic SIRS and how would you differentiate it? — Requires linking epidemiology, rapid test, and parasite smear.
Why is aggressive fluid resuscitation preferred over early vasopressors in SIRS? — Tests knowledge of perfusion physiology and resource‑limited practice.
Which antimicrobial regimen would you choose empirically in a rural Tanzanian hospital for SIRS of unknown origin? — Assesses awareness of local resistance patterns and drug availability.
What red‑flag laboratory value would prompt you to call for senior review? — Highlights lactate, creatinine, and persistent hypotension.
Explain how SIRS can progress to septic shock and the pathophysiologic mechanisms involved. — Connects inflammatory cascade to vasodilation and capillary leak.
When is it appropriate to stop antibiotics in a patient who met SIRS criteria but cultures are negative? — Tests stewardship and clinical judgement.
ai.title: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: SIRS is a physiologic response to a non‑specific insult that can progress to sepsis or organ failure. Recognising the criteria, common tropical triggers and early management saves lives in low‑resource settings.

b: Two or more criteria = SIRS
Does not require infection; any severe insult can trigger it
sections.p: SIRS is defined by the presence of two or more of the following: temperature >38 °C or <36 °C, heart rate ≥90 bpm, respiratory rate ≥20 bpm or PaCO₂ ≤32 mmHg, white‑cell count >12 000/µL, <4 000/µL, or >10 % bands.

b: Stage 1: SIRS alone
Stage 2: Sepsis (SIRS + infection)
Stage 3: Severe sepsis (organ dysfunction)
Stage 4: Septic shock (vasopressor need, lactate >2 mmol/L)
sections.p: SIRS is the first tier of the sepsis continuum. When infection is proven, it becomes sepsis; with organ dysfunction it is severe sepsis; with refractory shock, septic shock.

b: Malaria, severe bacterial pneumonia, typhoid, urinary‑tract infection, tuberculosis
HIV‑related opportunistic infections, malaria‑associated hemolysis
Severe malaria, dengue, viral hepatitis, schistosomiasis
Trauma, burns, major surgery, obstetric hemorrhage, severe anemia, sickle‑cell crisis
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent precipitants are infections common to the tropics, followed by non‑infectious insults.

b: Fever or low temperature
Rapid pulse and breathing
Altered mental status in later stages
Warm, flushed skin early; cool, mottled skin later
sections.p: Patients are usually febrile or hypothermic, tachycardic, tachypneic and may look ill‑appearing with warm extremities early on; later they can become hypotensive and confused.
Targeted tests confirm the trigger, assess organ function and guide therapy.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis, leukopenia or left shift? Helps confirm inflammatory response and may hint at infection type
Identify causative organism; if unavailable, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics based on local patterns

t.a: Rapid malaria test or thick smear
t.b: Detect malaria as a common trigger; positive result directs antimalarial therapy
Elevated >2 mmol/L signals tissue hypoperfusion; guides urgency of resuscitation
Assess renal function and electrolyte disturbances; rising creatinine indicates organ dysfunction
Look for pneumonia, TB, pleural effusion; informs antimicrobial choice

b: Persistent hypotension despite fluid bolus
Lactate >4 mmol/L
Acute kidney injury (creatinine rise >0.5 mg/dL)
Altered consciousness or seizures
sections.p: Progression to severe sepsis or septic shock carries high mortality, especially when organ failure develops.

b: Give 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus; repeat if MAP <65 mmHg
Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + gentamicin) within 1 hour; adjust for malaria, TB, HIV opportunists
Add antimalarial (artesunate) if rapid test positive
Monitor urine output, mental status, vitals every hour
Avoid NSAIDs in renal dysfunction; avoid steroids unless adrenal insufficiency
sections.p: Early source control, fluid resuscitation, and appropriate antimicrobial or antiparasitic therapy are the cornerstones.

b: Repeat lactate and creatinine 6‑hourly until stable
Vaccinate against pneumococcus, influenza, hepatitis B
Educate on malaria prophylaxis and early care seeking
sections.p: After stabilisation, reassess daily for organ recovery, de‑escalate antibiotics based on cultures, and address underlying risk factors.

b: Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxic storm) – usually has tremor, exophthalmos
Anaphylaxis – associated with urticaria, airway edema, hypotension
Acute adrenal crisis – hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, severe hypotension
sections.p: Conditions that share fever, tachycardia and tachypnea can be mistaken for SIRS.

b: White‑cell count may be normal in early malaria or viral infection
Lactate can be low if patient is hypoventilating or sample delayed
sections.p: Certain laboratory values may be falsely normal early in the course.
